So perhaps this entire concept is maybe well researched and documented but it has seemed to help some people I know with time management so I thought that I'd share on the chance that it might help any of you.

See, I once read about how the human brain can only process one 'conversation' at any given time, so if someone is talking to you and you're reading a book that you have to focus on only one of them at any given time, this got me thinking as due to a couple of mental illnesses that I have (ADHD and aspergers) I tend to crave a sense of basically constantly getting as much information as possible (like playing a video game and listening to a TV show at the same time) so I applied this basic concept to my own habits and came to the conclusion that there are four unique 'stimuli' which our brains can process separately, but if left alone for too long will drive at least me crazy.

They are visual, audio, conversational, and interaction, and while you can say listen to two things but the result will likely become a bit of a jumble of both (so if you're listening to someone talk some random noise in the background might make it hard to tell what's being said without focusing on it), however if you're aware of this you can help multi-task by finding tasks that don't overlap in any of these stimuli, for example listening to an audio book fulfills audio and conversational, so you'd maybe want some mundane task to work on like sweeping or such which doesn't involve a lot of thought to be both visual and interactive. That said, it's important to note that, assuming that I'm not mistaken of course, that the 'conversational' stimuli is a bit broader than it might first seem, ANY form of 'communication' that's being processed will take it up, talking to someone will take it up as you're thinking/listening to what you're saying, trying to solve a difficult puzzle would also use it up as you are thinking and communicating to yourself to figure things out, and stuff like that, most of the time anything that is interactive will be conversational unless you're so familiar with it that the actions are basically automatic, and even then it might just be using so little of your conversational stimuli that it doesn't disturb any other tasks. Still, I at least have found it useful to be able to figure out not only how can I best get through say a boring part of a game, a TV show that's a bit slow, or even how to fill my time without going crazy because one of the parts of my brain is doing 'nothing' even if the rest are doing something.

Though, I do think that there may be a few more 'stimuli', like touch and taste/smell, but they seem to 'always' be doing something, like say feeling/smelling/tasting the air, even though it might be something you're so used to you don't notice I believe that's enough to keep it stimulated which is why I at least have never felt that I was bored because one of those was left doing nothing.

Apologies if I rambled a bit, just wanted to share if someone found these thoughts useful.
